During overload, the challenge is to adapt these limits while preserving that differentiation and avoiding oscillations. Building on programmable enforcement and intelligent orchestration, we propose an agentic control loop combining UPF telemetry with locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM) selection from a finite set of admissible rate candidates. Deterministic logic validates each selection and derives Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) updates. The evaluated runs show no oscillations or fallbacks and unchanged highest-priority rate limits. These observations establish configuration preservation; delivered per-class QoS protection remains unmeasured.

papers.title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
papers.summary: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $\Delta_0$ suffice for a $15(\Delta_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $\Theta(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(\Delta_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((\Delta_0+1)(d+\log(k/\eta)))$ slots with failure probability at most $\eta$; for fixed $\Delta_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/\eta))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

papers.title: Topology-Aware Handover Management for Service Continuity in LEO Satellite Networks
papers.summary: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites are expected to play a key role in sixth-generation (6G) non-terrestrial networks. The high mobility of LEO satellites necessitates frequent handovers (HOs), posing challenges to service continuity and availability for user equipment. Conventional methods based on handover margin (HOM) and time-to-trigger (TTT) have limited adaptability to time-varying channel conditions and do not explicitly account for the impact of feeder-link and ground station (GS) connectivity on HO interruption time. To address these limitations, this paper develops a topology-aware HO framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). The framework uses reference signal received power (RSRP), satellite--GS associations, remaining visibility time, and elevation angles to determine when to initiate an HO and which satellite to select. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed policy achieves a service availability of 99.32% at a minimum elevation angle of 40 degrees, exceeding that of optimized HOM--TTT (O-HT) and least-delay (LD) satellite selection by 1.67 and 1.41 percentage points, respectively. The policy maintains service availability above 97.52% as the minimum elevation angle increases to 55 degrees, demonstrating its ability to sustain high service availability under stricter elevation constraints.

papers.title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
papers.summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

papers.title: Collision-Resilient All-to-All Broadcast Scheduling in Underwater Acoustic Networks
papers.summary: This paper studies all-to-all broadcast scheduling for underwater swarms with collision-resilient physical layers that can decode asynchronously overlapping packets. Propagation-aware collision-free schedulers coordinate packet arrivals but do not account for this reception capability. We first design a data-driven neural reception model that captures per-interferer power and timing effects. The model improves prediction accuracy over SINR baselines while admitting an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. The resulting neural-network-embedded MILP (NN-MILP) optimizes transmission times while explicitly encoding schedule-dependent overlaps and the predictor's inference, enabling globally optimal scheduling for small-scale instances. For larger networks, a two-stage ant colony optimization (ACO) heuristic combines low-cost transmission-order search with neural-aware timing refinement. Simulation results show that ACO shortens broadcast rounds compared with existing schedulers. It approaches the NN-MILP optimum on small-scale instances while supporting larger networks at substantially lower computational cost.

papers.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
papers.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

papers.title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

papers.title: Mathematical foundations for symmetric programming and reasoning
papers.summary: We develop a mathematical abstraction for uniformly exploiting symmetries in programming and reasoning based on the mathematical proof principle `without-loss-of-generality' (w.l.o.g.). Given: group actions that describe symmetries of the input and the output; and a canoniser, which captures how arbitrary inputs get sent to canonical ones, our construction extends any function from the canonical inputs to the whole domain. We characterise the conditions on the canonisers which guarantee that the construction gives the unique equivariant (i.e. symmetry-preserving) extension. Furthermore, we adapt the construction to a dependently-typed setting, where it captures traditional symmetric w.l.o.g. arguments via the Curry-Howard correspondence. Finally, we extend the construction to algebraic data types, where the symmetries of the constructors both uniquely determine the symmetries of the data type and pave the way for efficient execution.

papers.title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
papers.summary: Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

papers.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

papers.title: FIRE: Failure Isolation and Reliability for Production-Connected Experiments at Scale
papers.summary: Pre-production changes are usually tested in isolated environments to prevent their side effects from reaching production. Some record-and-replay platforms allow a production-connected mode: candidate changes receive recorded production requests while selected downstream calls reach production dependencies. This improves fidelity before deployment, but it also introduces reliability risks. At hyperscale, experimental traffic can fan out across shared services, trigger latent defects, or send malformed input to systems serving user requests. In this paper, we show how production-connected experimentation can operate reliably in a large-scale recommendation serving system. To contain downstream effects without sacrificing realistic dependency behavior, the platform uses three complementary guardrails. Isolated tiers redirect replay traffic away from shared dependencies where replication is practical. Dependency monitors observe downstream health and experiment-attributed errors and terminate experiments after sustained violations. Traffic pinning limits experimental calls to a designated subset of downstream workers when full replication would require scarce capacity. Isolated ranking tiers process billions of replayed requests per day using under 1% of the corresponding serving capacity. Over 90 days, these tiers experienced more than 200,000 abnormal worker exits without directly affecting production-serving workers. During a separate three-month window, dependency monitors cancelled approximately 5% of experiments for the measured ranking service and accounted for 87% of its cancellations. Dependency-aware triggering also reduced code-review experiment executions by 25%. These results show that high-fidelity, production-connected experimentation can operate at scale when downstream effects are isolated where possible, bounded where necessary, and continuously monitored and attributed.

papers.title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments. XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback. We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26-3.75 times the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/xinfer.

papers.title: Towards Runtime-Aware Observability for Java Virtual Threads
papers.summary: OS-level observability tools join application requests to kernel events through the OS thread ID, assuming that a unit of work occupies one OS thread until it completes. Java virtual threads break this assumption: many virtual threads are multiplexed onto a few carrier threads, so a stable thread ID hides a changing unit of work, and the join fails silently. Existing virtual-thread-aware channels republish context or identity on every mount and unmount, and the JVMTI-based one pays this cost for the lifetime of the JVM, whether or not an observer is attached. We bind a 64-byte off-heap trace buffer to each virtual thread, at a fixed address for its lifetime, and publish the address to eBPF consumers through four USDT probes in a patched OpenJDK; a re-implemented JVMTI channel over the same buffer serves as a controlled comparison. The four-probe design attributed all 768 test markers correctly on both the content and the identity plane, while the naive two-probe design silently misattributes trace context. With no consumer attached, publication costs at most about 33 ns per transition; the remaining dormant cost is buffer allocation, about 0.37 microseconds per virtual thread, which is negligible on transition-heavy workloads but nearly doubles the cost of a creation-only microbenchmark. The JVMTI channel costs about 20% on transition-heavy workloads and about 1.8 microseconds per virtual thread on the creation-only one. We also show that, of the two update strategies OTEP 4947 permits, only in-place rewriting guarded by the record's valid flag is sound for readers that cache the record's address, as lifecycle-event readers do.

papers.title: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation
papers.summary: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is. This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.

papers.title: Instruction-Aware Transfer of GPU Implementation Crossovers: a Tensor-Product Discontinuous Galerkin Operator on GB200, H100, and A100
papers.summary: We compare up to six implementations of an FP64 tensor-product discontinuous Galerkin operator at p = 7-1023 on GB200, H100, and A100 with fixed numerics, input, and code. The fastest path is machine dependent: at p = 511, a fused-epilogue GEMM path is 5.0% faster than a fused Tensor Core kernel on GB200 and 6.9% slower on A100. Nominal-peak scaling reproduces the A100 ranking but fails on H100, where the cost of FP64 arithmetic in the profiler-defined FP64 budget depends on the instruction. We therefore price each issued instruction at its architecture-dependent cost in that budget, using a calibration-side counter profile and one derived calibration factor per kernel, with no fit to the target. A retrospective leave-one-GPU-out evaluation, holding out target timings and counters but not the model form, transfers the p >= 511 path times with 1.9% median error at the common MMA shape, and the direction of the crossover at the H100 shape. Restricting the streaming multiprocessors of one A100, with nothing fitted, reproduces the A100-to-GB200 reversal. At roduction-relevant orders the model does not resolve the fastest fused path; the result identifies the crossover mechanism.

papers.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
papers.summary: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting

papers.title: Rateless Coding for Efficient Model Broadcast in Federated Learning
papers.summary: Model broadcast in federated learning (FL) with wireless channels faces significant challenges due to large model sizes and heterogeneous, unreliable channel conditions. While rateless coding has been widely adopted in modern broadcast communications to handle channel heterogeneity, its potential for model broadcast in FL remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we propose a joint source-channel coding scheme based on rateless coding to improve the robustness and efficiency of downlink model broadcast in FL. Specifically, we establish a rigorous convergence analysis of FL to inform the rateless code and quantization design under noisy downlink channel conditions. Moreover, by observing that the iterative process of FL naturally provides prior information about client updates, we leverage client-side local models as conditional prior information to aid the decoding process, thereby reducing transmission costs. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our rateless coding scheme significantly enhances downlink model broadcast efficiency in FL, while retaining comparable training accuracies for both homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions.

papers.title: A Parallel Greedy Algorithm for Maximal b-Matching in Hypergraphs
papers.summary: We present \parallelBatchBMatch, a parallel batch-vote algorithm for maximal $b$-matching in hypergraphs. The algorithm is deterministic for a given ordering of edges and produces the same output as the sequential greedy algorithm, i.e., the lexicographically first maximal $b$-matching. Under a uniformly random priority order it performs $O(m')$ expected work in the binary fork--join model, where $m'$ is the number of pins, the total number of vertex--edge incidences. The algorithm performs at most $m$ rounds for every priority order, where $m$ is the number of edges. Every round of the algorithm has $O(\log^2 m')$ depth with high probability, and thus the total depth of the algorithm is $O(m \log^2 m')$ with high probability. We implement the parallel algorithm in CUDA and evaluate it on real-world hypergraphs with capacities $b \in \{1, 3, 5\}$. The parallel algorithm computes the same matchings as the greedy algorithms and for the case of $b = 5$ it is up to $19.07$ times faster than the existing state-of-the art greedy algorithm.

papers.title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
papers.summary: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.

papers.title: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.

papers.title: What Does It Cost to Force-Close a Lightning Channel? Evidence from 974,000 Channel Closes, 2018-2026
papers.summary: Bitcoin's Lightning payment network returns the funds of a channel that cannot close cooperatively through pre-signed transactions whose fees and delays fall on its operators. That fee design is being replaced: Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed the mempool rule anchor channels relied on, and the Lightning specification adopted zero-fee commitments in May 2026. What the old design costs has never been measured across fee regimes. We trace every public channel close and every force close on-chain from January 2018 to October 2026, 973,581 closes, and follow each output to its spend. A separate chain index confirms all 698,476 public closes we could compare. Fee spikes did not bring a wave of force closes. Force closes in a spike week and the next were 0.97 times the four weeks before, against 1.02 after ordinary weeks of the same years. A force close costs 2-6 times a cooperative close in fees and locks the closer's balance for days, which outweighs the fees only in low-fee years. When fees are high, pending payments are exposed: in 2023, 18.2% of HTLC timeouts confirmed more than 40 blocks after expiry. Yet since 2021, forwarding nodes lost only 38 payments, each with the preimage already on-chain. Anchor outputs cut late timeouts in fee spikes (20.6% against 30.5%), yet owners rarely bump commitments with them, and miners take most of what third parties sweep. Zero-fee commitments would save only 12% of the anchor mechanism's block space; they should be judged by how promptly payments resolve when fees spike.

papers.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
papers.summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.

papers.title: Control-Flow Profiling for Workload Representativeness
papers.summary: Workload characterization in performance engineering often replaces expensive target executions with lower-cost proxies, including reduced datasets, miniapps, and training inputs. Such substitutions require empirical verification that the proxy faithfully exercises the target's dynamic execution behavior. This paper presents an address-keyed control-flow profiling methodology and tool suite designed to evaluate workload representativeness directly from compiled, unmodified binaries. We pair time-ordered basic-block vector (BBV) recurrence analysis with exp-branchprof, an experimental Valgrind tool that captures five orthogonal structural profile families spanning branch direction bias, four-bit global history contexts, dynamic indirect targets, function call transitions, and intraprocedural CFG edges. Our method compares weighted event distributions from two executions of the same binary. It reports support coverage, reference event-mass coverage, distribution distance, entropy-derived quantities, and phase structure, rather than claiming that a single similarity score certifies a proxy. We validate the tool with exact-oracle microbenchmarks across AArch64 and x86-64, covering conditional and inverted exits, calls, returns, direct and indirect jumps, and forked processes. We then apply the workflow to SPEC CPU2017 and CPU2026 train/reference pairs and seven refrate/refspeed pairs. The corpus contains both close matches and cases where a shorter execution reaches much of the same code but misses substantial target, callgraph, CFG, or BBV event mass. The accompanying artifact supports the same analysis for proprietary workload/proxy pairs without requiring raw PC-level profiles to leave the collection environment.

papers.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
papers.summary: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

papers.title: Graded Intersection Types
papers.summary: We introduce graded intersection types, in which arrow domains are multisets of types with coefficients in a semiring. Boolean and natural number grades recover idempotent and non-idempotent intersection types. We give algebraic conditions on the semiring for subject reduction and expansion in finite systems and in locally finite systems with guarded infinite types. We construct a lifting to multisets of grades corresponding, in this general setting, to lifting the idempotent system to the non-idempotent one. We recall the main existing operational characterisations from the literature, and show some general extensions.

papers.title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
papers.summary: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

papers.title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution
papers.summary: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth pose significant challenges for efficient inference. Pruning during training often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to significantly reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity efficiently at runtime remains challenging due to irregular memory access patterns and workload imbalance across processing elements. In this work, we investigate the standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance characteristics through roofline analysis, showing that a 3 x 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of approximately 10 FLOP/byte compared to roughly 96 FLOP/byte for its dense counterpart. We propose techniques for an efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach achieves upto 1.65x speedup as compared to dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and upto 1.52x on NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1) , motivating further exploration of direct convolution as a practical path to efficient sparse inference on modern accelerators/edge devices.

papers.title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
papers.summary: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

papers.title: Toward Optimal-Complexity Hash-Based Asynchronous MVBA with Optimal Resilience
papers.summary: Multi-valued validated Byzantine agreement (MVBA), a fundamental primitive of distributed computing, allows $n$ processes to agree on a valid $\ell$-bit value, despite $t$ faulty processes behaving maliciously. Among hash-based solutions for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults, the state-of-the-art HMVBA protocol achieves optimal $O(n^2)$ message complexity, (near-)optimal $O(n \ell + n^2 \lambda \log n)$ bit complexity, and optimal $O(1)$ time complexity. However, it only tolerates $t < \frac15 n$ failures. In contrast, the best-known optimally-resilient protocol, SQ, incurs a higher bit complexity of $O(n^2 \ell + n^3 \lambda)$. This poses a fundamental question: Can a hash-based protocol be designed for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults that simultaneously achieves optimal complexity and optimal resilience? This paper takes a significant step toward answering this question. Namely, we introduce Reducer, an MVBA protocol that retains HMVBA's optimal complexity while improving its resilience to $t < \frac14 n$. Like HMVBA and SQ, Reducer relies exclusively on collision-resistant hash functions. A key innovation in Reducer's design is its internal use of strong multi-valued Byzantine agreement (SMBA), a new variant of Byzantine agreement we introduce and construct, which ensures that the decided value was proposed by a correct process. To further advance resilience toward the optimal one-third bound, we then propose Reducer++, an MVBA protocol that tolerates up to $t < (\frac13 - \epsilon)n$ adaptive failures, for any fixed constant $\epsilon > 0$. Unlike Reducer, Reducer++ does not rely on SMBA. Instead, it employs a novel approach involving hash functions modeled as random oracles to ensure termination. Reducer++ maintains constant time complexity, quadratic message complexity, and quasi-quadratic bit complexity, with constants dependent on $\epsilon$.

papers.title: Versatile yet Efficient Network Traffic Analysis: Offloading Network Foundation Model to SmartNIC
papers.summary: Pervasive encryption makes large-scale labeling infeasible for traffic analysis, while security operations demand edge analysis to avert service degradation and vulnerabilities. These pressures have produced two research lines that advance 1) versatile analysis, via network foundation models for low label dependency, and 2) efficient analysis, via hardware offloading for low analysis latency. However, co-achieving versatility and efficiency via such lines has appeared incompatible, with prior work advancing one while compromising the other, yet we show that this incompatibility is a consequence of polarized design choices across the three components of traffic analysis systems, i.e., traffic processing, model architecture, and analysis execution. In response, we present Nepco, a versatile yet efficient network traffic analysis system that offloads network foundation models to SmartNIC. Our key observation is that discriminative traffic information often exhibits localized patterns within byte sequences, motivating versatile yet efficient localized byte-sequence modeling. To exploit this without incurring the latency bottlenecks of complex encoding steps, we employ a hardware-friendly processing strategy that directly embeds raw byte sequences. To maintain versatility across diverse tasks characterized by spatially shifting features, we explore an observation-driven convolution architecture equipped with hardware-friendly scoring and gating designs. By exploiting translation invariance, this design dynamically locates and extracts salient semantic signatures irrespective of their byte-level offsets. We prototype Nepco on the NVIDIA BlueField-3 SmartNIC with multi-engine collaborative analysis execution. The experimental results demonstrate that Nepco achieves macro F1 competitive with the best performances achieved by 8 state-of-the-art network foundation models...

papers.title: Batched Early-Exit LLM Inference Done Right with DREX
papers.summary: Early-exit (EE) LLMs let confident tokens skip a model's deep layers, but batched serving loses most of this gain. Current systems either force tokens to exit before their own ramp is confident, an error the ramp does not bound, or save almost nothing when decoding is weight-bound, because any continuing token makes a step read the deep weights. We present DREX, a batched EE serving system that never forces a token to exit. DREX introduces cross-iteration batching: tokens that continue past the exit layer wait there, and every few steps one deep pass over all waiting tokens reads the deep weights once for several steps. Its two policies differ in what such a token's request does: holding pauses it until the deep pass, and speculative holding lets it keep decoding from the exit layer's own guess, which the next deep pass verifies. Exited tokens are trusted and never verified. Using a calibrated cost model, a controller picks speculative holding where reading weights dominates a step and guesses are often right, and holding elsewhere. DREX keeps vLLM's asynchronous scheduling by planning each deep pass from exit counts of earlier steps. With synthetic exits where 90% of tokens exit at a quarter of the depth and 40% of guesses are correct, DREX achieves 2.22-2.24$\times$ decode speedup over non-EE across batch sizes on Llama-2-70B, while per-row skipping (vSkipper's design) gains at most 7.0%. On LayerSkip models, DREX adds no statistically resolved quality loss to the EE model's own. On CNN/DM at full memory, DREX with LayerSkip achieves 1.58-1.91$\times$ decode speedup while remaining within 1.4 ROUGE-2 points of the non-EE model. These speedups are 9-63% larger than EAGLE's across the evaluated model sizes, with each method measured against its own non-EE target.

papers.title: Prophecy Variables, Program Analysis, Binding Times, and Staged Compilation in the BuildIt System
papers.summary: BuildIt is a lightweight C++ library system for implementing domain specific languages (DSLs) and compilers through multi-stage execution. It uses partial evaluation to generate optimized code without requiring parsers, explicit intermediate representations (IRs), or custom code generators. History variables and forward execution support analyses of past computation, but optimizations such as data movement, operator fusion, and binding-time analysis also require information about future execution. We introduce prophecy variables into BuildIt to predict future program behavior and guide code generation. Repeated first-stage execution refines predictions until they satisfy the program's checks, extending BuildIt's existing reexecution machinery with little additional complexity. This approach obtains information typically computed by backwards dataflow analyses over an explicit IR while preserving BuildIt's lightweight implementation model. The cost of first-stage reexecution can be amortized over repeated executions of the generated code. We formalize the mechanism and mechanize its guarantees in Lean 4. We demonstrate prophecy variables in three applications: selective CPU-GPU data movement, neural-network operator fusion, and automatic binding-time analysis. These applications achieve performance improvements of up to 5.5x while simplifying the programming interface.

papers.title: BOA Constrictor: Squeezing Performance out of GPUs in the Cloud via Budget-Optimal Allocation
papers.summary: The past decade has seen a dramatic increase in demand for GPUs to train Machine Learning (ML) models. Because it is prohibitively expensive for most organizations to build and maintain a large GPU cluster, organizations instead choose to rent GPUs from cloud providers. The customer is responsible for devising a policy for (i) deciding how many GPUs to rent at every moment in time to process a stream of ML training jobs and (ii) allocating the rented GPUs among the currently active jobs in the system. Because ML training jobs can be parallelized across different numbers of GPUs, the customer generally has many options for how many GPUs to use for each job. Allocating more GPUs to a single training job will cause the job to complete more quickly. However, the customer pays for each GPU-hour they use, and a training job receives a diminishing marginal benefit from running on additional GPUs. Hence, allocating too many GPUs to a single training job can dramatically increase the overall cost that the customer pays to the cloud provider. This gives rise to a cost-performance tradeoff that customers must balance when running training jobs in the cloud. To balance the cost-performance tradeoff, we develop BOA Constrictor, a new scheduler for ML training jobs which uses a Budget-Optimal Allocation (BOA) policy to squeeze the highest level of performance out of a cloud-deployed GPU cluster given a fixed budget constraint. We explicitly formulate the problem as a budget-constrained scheduling problem and derive the BOA policy which minimizes the average job completion time (JCT) of a stream of arriving jobs subject to the user's budget. For a given budget level, we demonstrate that BOA Constrictor can reduce average JCT by 1.6 times in small-scale implementation experiments and by 2 times in detailed, large-scale simulations compared to state-of-the-art heuristic based schedulers.

papers.title: Mean field optimal Core Allocation across Malleable jobs
papers.summary: Modern data centers and cloud computing clusters are increasingly running workloads composed of malleable jobs. A malleable job can be parallelized across any number of cores, yet the job typically exhibits diminishing marginal returns for each additional core on which it runs. Examples of malleable jobs include machine learning tasks, parallelized across multiple GPUs, and large-scale database queries, parallelized across multiple servers. Given the prevalence of malleable jobs, theoretical works have posed the problem of how to allocate a fixed number of cores across a stream of arriving malleable jobs so as to minimize the mean response time across jobs. We refer to this as the Core Allocation to Malleable jobs (CAM) problem. Although quite a few recent papers have been written on CAM, the problem remains challenging to solve optimally. In particular, prior theoretical work has only solved the CAM problem in very constrained cases. This paper takes a new approach to CAM, looking at the problem in the mean field asymptotic regime. In this regime, we are able to optimally solve a much more general instance of CAM. We derive two distinct mean field optimal policies, FW-CAM and GLAM. FW-CAM demonstrates a new intuition: in the mean field regime, individual job sizes are not relevant in finding an optimal policy. GLAM (Gittins-Like Allocation for Malleable jobs) is asymptotically optimal under certain common assumptions, and also serves as a good heuristic outside of the asymptotic regime by adapting dynamically to the current number of jobs in the system. Notably, none of the policies previously proposed in the literature are mean field optimal when jobs follow different speedup functions.

papers.title: Pending Conflicts Make Progress Impossible
papers.summary: In this work, we study progress conditions for commutativity-aware, linearizable implementations of shared objects. Motivated by the observation that commuting operations can be executed in parallel, we introduce conflict-obstruction-freedom: a process is guaranteed to complete its operation if it runs for long enough without encountering step contention with conflicting (non-commuting) operations. This condition generalizes obstruction-freedom and wait-freedom by allowing progress as long as step contention is only induced by commuting operations. We prove that conflict-obstruction-free universal constructions are impossible to implement in the asynchronous read-write shared memory model. This result exposes a fundamental limitation of conflict-aware universal constructions: the mere invocation of conflicting operations imposes a synchronization cost. Progress requires eventual resolution of pending conflicts.

papers.title: Contract-Theoretic Semantic Abstraction for Covert Communication in LAENets
papers.summary: In Low-Altitude Economy Networks (LAENets), Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) transmit task-related information to the Base Station (BS) under stringent low-probability-of-detection constraints. These constraints limit transmission resources, hindering reliable information delivery through conventional bit-level communication. Semantic Communication (SemCom) addresses this challenge by prioritizing task-relevant information over bit-level accuracy. However, semantic abstraction must balance information loss and redundancy to preserve task reliability and transmission efficiency. Moreover, the BS cannot directly observe or reliably verify UAVs' semantic processing capabilities and abstraction-dependent transmission costs, leading to information asymmetry. We propose an incentive-aware semantic abstraction framework for covert communications in LAENets. Specifically, we adjust UAV-side semantic abstraction levels to provide differentiated covert semantic services under fixed-dimensional transmission payloads. To address information asymmetry, we develop a contract-theoretic model and adopt Prospect Theory (PT) to capture risk-sensitive semantic abstraction decisions under uncertainty. We further design a Regularized Diffusion-based Soft Actor-Critic (RDSAC) algorithm for optimal contract design under PT, incorporating diffusion entropy and action entropy regularization. Numerical results validate the proposed framework and show that RDSAC improves average rewards by 6.77% over SAC and 31.78% over proximal policy optimization.

papers.title: Lightweight GenAI for Network Traffic Generation: Fidelity, Augmentation, and Classification
papers.summary: Network Traffic Classification (NTC) increasingly relies on data-driven models, yet its practical deployment is often constrained by limited labeled data, strict privacy requirements, and the cost of collecting representative traffic traces. While Network Traffic Generation (NTG) provides an effective means to mitigate data scarcity, conventional generative methods struggle to model the complex temporal dynamics of modern traffic and often incur high computational costs. In this article, we investigate lightweight Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) architectures for practical NTG. Rather than generating raw packet bytes or relying on large foundation models, we synthesize compact flow-level traffic representations derived from early packet-header information, enabling transformer-based, state-space, and diffusion models with only a few million parameters. We present a modular GenAI pipeline for NTG and evaluate it along four complementary axes: (i) synthetic traffic fidelity, (ii) synthetic-only training for reduced raw-data sharing in NTC, (iii) data augmentation under low-data regimes, and (iv) computational efficiency. Experiments on two heterogeneous datasets show that lightweight transformer-based and state-space models preserve both static and temporal traffic characteristics, while providing useful synthetic data for downstream NTC. Among them, transformer-based models offer the best fidelity-efficiency trade-off, combining high-quality traffic generation with moderate computational overhead.

papers.title: GPUOS: A GPU Operating System Primitive for Transparent Operation Fusion
papers.summary: Modern deep learning workloads often consist of many small tensor operations, especially in inference, attention, and micro-batched training. In these settings, kernel launch overhead can become a major bottleneck, sometimes exceeding the actual computation time. We present GPUOS, a GPU runtime JIT system that reduces launch overhead using a persistent kernel architecture with runtime operator injection. GPUOS runs a single long-lived GPU kernel that continuously processes tasks from a host-managed work queue, eliminating repeated kernel launches. To support diverse operations, GPUOS uses NVIDIA NVRTC to just-in-time compile operators at runtime and inject them into the running kernel through device function pointer tables. This design enables operator updates without restarting the kernel or recompiling the system. GPUOS introduces four key ideas: (1) a persistent worker kernel with atomic task queues, (2) a runtime operator injection mechanism based on NVRTC and relocatable device code, (3) a dual-slot aliasing scheme for safe concurrent operator updates, and (4) transparent PyTorch integration through TorchDispatch that batches micro-operations into unified submissions. The system supports arbitrary tensor shapes, strides, data types, and broadcasting through a generic tensor abstraction. Experiments show that GPUOS achieves up to 15.3x speedup over standard PyTorch on workloads dominated by small operations, including micro-batched inference and attention patterns. GPUOS improves utilization while remaining compatible with the PyTorch ecosystem.

papers.title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
papers.summary: Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue. We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/MARS_preview .

papers.title: Idleness is Relative: Exploiting Tool-Call Idle Windows for Offloading in Agentic Systems with MORI
papers.summary: Agentic programs alternate between LLM inference and tool calls, each request extending the previous one's context. Program-aware schedulers pin a program's KV cache in GPU HBM across tool calls to avoid re-prefilling it at every step, but as contexts grow, pinned KV cache exceeds HBM, raising program eviction: deciding when a program releases GPU memory and when it returns. Offloading to CPU DRAM lets an evicted program wait out a tool call instead of recomputing its context, but existing schedulers leave DRAM to LRU, so offloaded programs thrash. Making these decisions is hard: tool-call durations vary by orders of magnitude and are unknown in advance. We observe that programs nevertheless stay busy (short tool calls) or idle (long ones) for extended periods, and use a program's idleness, its recent fraction of time in tool calls, as a continuous, relative metric. MORI ranks programs by idleness, keeps the least idle in HBM and the next in DRAM, and drops the rest, enforcing admission control at both tiers under any GPU-to-CPU capacity ratio; it also proactively demotes idle programs to make room for ready ones. On real coding-agent traces, MORI achieves on average 64% higher throughput and 72% lower p90 TTFT than the best offloading baseline under high load.

papers.title: Duet: Co-Optimizing P2P Message Propagation and Rotating-Leader Consensus
papers.summary: In blockchain systems, peer-to-peer (P2P) overlay networks play a crucial role in providing reliable, scalable and efficient message-delivery services to upper layers. However, the consensus layer and the underlying P2P network remain mutually opaque in existing blockchains, waiving the opportunity for further improvement. In contrast to other P2P applications, blockchain can naturally be abstracted as a state machine. We therefore leverage this abstraction to record network topologies and latencies in a trusted and coordinated manner. With this support, we propose three improvements to rotating-leader consensus protocols and their underlying P2P networks: (1) accelerating leader rotation; (2) introducing a reliable-broadcast paradigm that employs tree-based dissemination in the normal case and falls back to gossip only when necessary; and (3) constructing latency-aware dissemination trees. We integrate the above ideas into Tendermint and libp2p, and conduct empirical evaluation on Amazon EC2 platform using up to 300 nodes distributed across 10 regions. The results demonstrate that, compared with gossip-based dissemination over the same topology, our prototype improves peak throughput by up to $7.26\times$.

papers.title: ASAP: Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode Refinement For Binary Decompilation
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in binary decompilation to refine the C-like pseudocode produced by traditional rule-based decompilers. While this pseudocode is useful, it is a heuristic and lossy abstraction rather than a faithful copy of the source code. It often contains decompiler errors, especially for aggressively optimized binaries where critical low-level details are obscured. We present ASAP, an Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode refinement framework for binary decompilation. ASAP learns source-aligned assembly representations from paired source and binary functions using joint function-level and snippet-level contrastive alignment. A Q-Former then compresses chunk-level assembly features into a fixed number of assembly tokens. These tokens and the decompiler-produced pseudocode jointly condition the decompilation LLM. During refinement, we use stochastic pseudocode masking and a relative assembly-advantage loss to discourage the model from relying solely on pseudocode. On two decompilation benchmarks across multiple compiler optimization levels, ASAP improves the average re-execution rate from 64.7% to 71.9% and the average recompilation rate from 91.6% to 96.6% compared with the strongest baseline. Our approach offers both a new perspective and a practical solution to binary decompilation.

papers.title: A Simplified Layout Algebra for GPU Kernels
papers.summary: The layout algebra behind NVIDIA's CuTe library describes how tensor tiles map onto threads and memory. A layout is a shape with a stride for each entry, so a coordinate's address is the sum of its indices times their strides. As formalized by Shah and by Cecka, its central operations (e.g., composition, complement, division, product) are guarded by at least six interacting admissibility conditions. We show that this complexity is an artifact of a representational choice, not of the domain. We present a layout algebra in which every layout names the space its inputs and outputs live in: logical, physical, or thread-value indices. A layout into logical or thread-value space must be a bijection from its $N$ coordinates onto $[0,N)$. A layout into physical space must be alias-free: distinct coordinates land on distinct addresses, except under broadcast, where many threads read one value on purpose and the layout must mark where. Nothing maps out of a physical index. Composing $f$ with $g$ requires only that $f$'s range be exactly $g$'s flattened coordinate set. The index arithmetic can always be emitted naively: compute $f$, split the result by division and remainder into $g$'s coordinates, and apply $g$. Often the composite simplifies to a layout; we show that when it does, there is a coarsest such form, whose digits every other one refines, and we emit that. A warp's or thread's slice is a \emph{restriction}. A restricted layout is no longer composable, which forces the user to settle the whole view of a tile before taking slices. We validate the algebra by reproducing within it CuTe's operations, such as composition, complement, and division. We implement it in OCaml and use the implementation to rederive CuTe's atoms and usage patterns. The decision procedure is proved correct in Rocq.

papers.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.

papers.title: When Does Blockwise Additivity Break? Diagnosing and Repairing the Additive Assumption in Distillation-Based Architecture Search
papers.summary: Blockwise distillation methods for architecture search, such as DNA, DONNA, LANA and Puzzle, score each candidate replacement block in isolation and combine the scores additively. We ask at which budgets this additivity assumption fails, whether fine-tuning repairs the failure, what diagnoses it, and how it can be repaired cheaply. On DeiT-S, DeiT-B, Swin-T and Qwen2.5-0.5B with seven latency budgets each, an additive integer program trails a pairwise interaction-aware program after fine-tuning by at most 1.6 top-1 points on ImageNet-1k at the mildest budgets, but by up to 17.5 points, and a factor of 1.9 in perplexity, at aggressive ones. After 10,000 fine-tuning steps 3.3-9.9 points remain on DeiT, whereas on Swin-T the gap shrinks to at most about 1.8 points within 500 steps. In a learning-rate sweep with the standard 2,000 steps, 6.0-10.7 points remain on DeiT when each method's rate is chosen by its evaluation-set accuracy. An intervention that keeps the block library and only forbids more than two removals in any three adjacent layers shrinks the DeiT gap from 5.8-17.5 to 0.7-5.2 points, mostly by improving the additive solution: adjacent removals are a major failure pattern. Splitting the additivity error into a metric and a functional part, relative to additive logit changes, indicates where a cheap logit-sum predictor can be trusted. A hybrid search that ranks moves with this predictor and measures only the best needs no pair measurements and, after Holm adjustment, is significantly better than the pairwise program in 10 of 14 ImageNet-1k settings, with no statistically significant losses. An ablation shows that its ranking helps except at the most aggressive DeiT-B budget, where the predictor misleads and random ranking or ten-times-costlier evolution does better.

papers.title: Characterizing CUDA Locality Domains on Blackwell GPUs
papers.summary: Low latency is critical to user experience. As NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin GPUs advance multi-die scaling, data placement and cross-die communication become increasingly important. However, the latency implications and underlying costs of cross-die communication and die-aware execution remain largely unexplored. In this report, we present a comprehensive evaluation of the Locality Domain (LD) feature introduced in CUDA 13.4. Conducted on a single node equipped with eight NVIDIA B300 GPUs, our study examines three aspects: memory management and access, computation, and communication, to identify the sources of latency and, more importantly, explore how LD can mitigate them. Our measurements show that the benefits of LD depend on data access patterns. Through die-aware adaptations and integration with widely used libraries and tools, we achieve speedups of up to 43.5% for NCCL 2.32.3 (AllGather), 111.3% for nvbandwidth (DtoD), and 37% for DeepGEMM (EP). We also identify non-negligible LD-related GPU memory allocation overhead when allocation sizes exceed 32 MB due to barrier and TLB invalidation, we propose a fix to the GPU driver kernel module (submitted to NVIDIA) and show that overhead could be reduced 7x ~ 10x without requiring any user-code changes.

papers.title: SymFC: Configurable Semantics for All Paths Symbolic Execution in Haskell via Embeddings
papers.summary: Lightweight methods like QuickCheck have proven to be successful in functional languages and beyond, as they let users specify properties as Boolean functions directly in code. We can replicate some of their benefits for (bounded) proofs via symbolic execution. If we can execute arbitrary functions symbolically, we can specify properties just as easily. Unfortunately, existing symbolic execution tools for Haskell are restricted to a subset of the language that excludes many real-world applications like IO; they also have a hard time scaling to larger programs, making them a poor fit for general purpose lightweight verification. One reason behind these limitations is that existing techniques only offer fixed symbolic semantics for SMT base types. This makes it hard to cover more programming constructs and libraries; it also makes it difficult to fine-tune symbolic representations for better performance. We present SymFC, a new symbolic execution method for Haskell that offers configurable semantics via embeddings. An embedding of a function in SymFC is just another Haskell function that can use arbitrary code, as well as SMT primitives. Embeddings make it easy to support new programming constructs and fine-tune symbolic representations for speed. To integrate embeddings into Haskell's type system, we make use of Haskell's coercions, which let us transparently convert between a Haskell type and the type of its embedding. We realize embeddings in SymFC, an all-paths symbolic execution engine for Haskell, which lets us symbolically represent arbitrary types and values in GHC core. We implement SymFC as a GHC plugin, and evaluate it by checking properties of Haskell's container library, and the iproute library. We build embeddings for IORef, Haskell's Ptr/ForeignPtr interface, and the hardware library Clash, and our evaluation reports a 6.25x speedup on G2's own benchmarks.

papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.

papers.title: PENSA: A Spatial Accelerator for BitNet b1.58 Inference on an HBM-equipped AMD Alveo FPGA
papers.summary: Ternary large language models (tLLMs) replace general multiplication in dominant linear layers with sign-controlled accumulation, shifting hardware bottlenecks toward packed-weight delivery, reduction, and operator occupancy. PENSA is an end-to-end FPGA accelerator for the BitNet b1.58 2B4T model on an AMD Alveo U50. Two row-partitioned ternary matrix engines consume packed TQ1_0 weights from eight independent high-bandwidth memory (HBM) pseudo-channels, each processing 1,280 ternary weights per cycle through sign selection and integer reduction. The sequencer, attention, and vocabulary-projection units remain resident on the FPGA, while two-stream interleaved scheduling overlaps sequences across the persistent pipeline to form the Penta-Unit. At 104.1~MHz, PENSA achieves 58.09 tok/s at context 128 and 24.60 tok/s at context 2048, corresponding to 2.14-3.14$\times$ the throughput of a same-model Xeon E-2356G baseline. The resulting system demonstrates end-to-end FPGA execution of 2B-scale BitNet topology without modifying its model structure.

papers.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

papers.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
papers.summary: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework. We open-source the system implementation of Evolving Infra at https://github.com/mit-han-lab/EvolvingInfra.

papers.title: Release Sooner, Expose Less: Offloading MoE Dispatch in NCCL-EP under Dual-Batch Overlap
papers.summary: Dual-batch overlap (DBO) hides mixture-of-experts (MoE) communication behind another microbatch's computation, but only after dispatch send releases the GPU. The time dispatch send holds the GPU therefore stays exposed, while network progress after release can be hidden. We evaluate GPUDirect Async - Kernel Initiated (GDA-KI) Free Flow, an NCCL-EP research configuration that leaves WQE construction on the GPU but moves send progression to a host thread. On a GB300 NVL72 system, GDA-KI Free Flow reduces dispatch-send time relative to default GDA-KI at every operating point in the evaluated parameter sweep. An experiment that inserts a GPU delay between dispatch send and receive shows that offload increases the in-flight interval. Depending on the load, 32-96 microseconds of computation or other independent work between send and receive hides the deferred progress, leaving less exposed time than default GDA-KI. In disaggregated vLLM serving with DBO, GDA-KI Free Flow lowers median TPOT by 15-25% relative to NCCL-EP default GDA-KI and by 16-42% relative to DeepEP v1.

papers.title: FedADMM-InSa: An Inexact and Self-Adaptive ADMM for Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) is a promising framework for learning from distributed data while maintaining privacy. The development of efficient FL algorithms encounters various challenges, including heterogeneous data and systems, limited communication capacities, and constrained local computational resources. Recently developed FedADMM methods show great resilience to both data and system heterogeneity.
